data.title: Nearly 80% of Small Business Owners Put Personal Money Into Their Business: Flute
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • 79% of small business owners put personal money into their businesses in the past year, often to cover inventory costs while they wait for payments to clear.
  • Just 4% of owners who needed cash turned to their payment processor, even though processors already see a business’s daily sales.

A new report from Flute finds that 79% of small business owners put personal money into their businesses in the past year.

The Cost of Waiting To Get Paid examines how small business owners, fund their businesses, how quickly they get paid, and what happens when cash runs dry.The report from the payments platform found that 57% of owners have $1,000 or more tied up in pending deposits, holds, or unpaid invoices at any given time.

More than half of owners (52%) needed extra cash in the past year, most often to buy inventory that must be paid for weeks before it sells. To cover cash shortfalls, owners turned to business credit cards (48%), bank loans (47%), and their own savings (42%).

Why Are Small Business Owners Using Personal Savings to Keep Operating?

Together, the findings show how owners rely on their own savings and credit to keep their businesses running while they wait for payments to reach their accounts, according to Derek Dean, CEO of Flute.

“A business can have a good week of sales and still need the owner’s savings to pay for the next inventory order,” said Dean in a statement. “If the money hasn’t landed by the time their bills come due, owners cover the wait out of their own pockets. Over time, that puts pressure on their household finances and on the business. Payment providers already know what a business is bringing in every day”

Why Can’t Small Business Owners Get the Financing They Need?

Thew report finds that despite many SBE owners needing financial help, that have never approached a lender— only 37% applied for financing, and 28% of applicants received less than they requested or were denied outright. Smaller businesses faced the greatest barriers. Among businesses with less than $250,000 in revenue that needed cash, 27% could not access funding, compared with 0% of the larger businesses. Payment processors already see a business’s daily sales, but few owners turn to them for funding. Among owners who needed cash, just 4% used their payment processor, making it the least-used funding source.

Waiting for money to reach the bank adds another layer of cash pressure. According to the report, 58% of owners wait two or more days for bank settlement, and 73% say faster access to their own money would meaningfully change how they run their business. Larger businesses are more likely to have substantial amounts tied up: 73% of businesses with at least $250,000 in revenue have $1,000 or more waiting to clear, compared with 42% of smaller businesses.

Moreover, slow customer payments affect day-to-day decisions. Nearly two-thirds of owners (63%) say those delays forced them to change how they operated in the past year, with 35% delaying inventory purchases and 28% using personal savings or credit to cover the wait. Owners are drawing on the same personal funds they turn to when financing falls short.
data.author: james.hickey

data.title: Before You Block the Bot, Find Out Who Sent It
data.description:
For years, you’ve trained your site to treat automated traffic as a threat. Bots buy up limited releases and test stolen cards. So when an AI agent arrives to place an order, your first instinct may be to shut it out. Some of those agents are working for your best customers.

In September 2026, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after the assistant launched, citing concerns about customer security and the shopping experience. Walmart took a different route in October: it announced a way for approved agents to shop on behalf of its customers. Both choices start from the same responsibility. You’re still the one who has to get the order right.

Consider Who You’d Turn Away

In September 2026, Adobe found that visits to U.S. retail sites from AI tools generated 83% more revenue per visit than traffic from other sources. Some of those shoppers are likely already your members, and I wouldn’t turn them away just because they sent an agent.

Check Which Agent is Asking

Keep the price and stock information an assistant can see as current as the information on your own site. Letting it check whether an item is in stock helps shoppers find you. Before it can pull up a customer’s order or place a new one, verify which agent is making the request and whether you’ve allowed it to take that action.

Walmart is taking that approach with the Agent Gateway it announced on October 21, 2026. Its developer beta is invitation-only. Walmart also described plans for a separate profile for each agent, linked to the shopper’s Walmart account. That gives the customer a way to see what an agent bought and to remove its access when they no longer want it shopping for them. Walmart gives $50, $100 and $200 as examples of spending limits a shopper can set for an agent.

Recognize the Customer

When a customer sends a friend to collect a curbside order, your staff don’t turn them away. They don’t hand over the bag to just anyone, either. They check the name and order number. An agent is that friend at the pickup counter.

Once you’ve checked the agent, you still need to know who sent it. When the shopper signs in and links their account, you get the same moment you’d have at the counter: “Oh, it’s Alex. I know him.” You can use the account Alex already has instead of making him check out as a guest.

Take a shopper who asks an assistant to reorder their usual cereal. They pay $4 in your app when they’re signed in. The basket in the chat shows $6. You can still make the sale at that price, but you’ve asked a regular to pay more because they came in through a different door.

Give Shoppers a Choice Before They Pay

They can sign in with you to connect the account they already have, or they can continue as a guest at the guest price. Your pricing system should decide what price applies. The assistant needs the price you’ll honor for that basket. It doesn’t need the customer’s purchase history to show the discount.

If a shopper doesn’t have an account, give them the option to join. A discount on their first order might make it worth signing up. Let them decide, and let them do it with you. A purchase through an assistant isn’t permission to enroll someone in your loyalty program.

If the channel can’t honor the member price, bring the shopper back to your checkout where you can. Carry the basket across and tell them why you’re sending them there. That’s better than making them rebuild the order or discover the difference on the receipt.

Let the Shopper Set the Limit

Knowing it’s Alex doesn’t tell you what Alex agreed to buy. If a shopper asks an assistant to reorder breakfast staples for up to $50 and a substitution puts the total at $54, the assistant should stop and ask.

The fact that it can see the member price doesn’t change the limit the shopper gave it.

I’d have your team decide which orders an assistant can place within a limit and when the shopper needs to approve the final basket. Keep a record of what the shopper approved with the order. If they call about a charge, your service team should be able to see what happened without asking them to dig through a chat.

Give the Order a Home After Checkout

Whether the sale finishes in the chat or on your site, signed-in customers should be able to find the order with their other purchases. If they want to change their delivery date or make a return, they should know they can come to you. Give guests a way to get help, too. Don’t count an order you can’t match as a new customer. It could be from someone who shops with you every week.

The next time something unfamiliar shows up at your store, don’t stop at asking whether to block it. Ask who sent it. It could be someone who already shops with you every week.

Click here to read our take on how retailers can welcome AI shoppers without losing the customer relationship.

Frank Maduri is President of LoginID, where he focuses on helping businesses recognize the person behind a digital interaction and understand what that person has authorized. An engineer by training, he previously led product at Rogers and worked on mobile wallets at BlackBerry.
data.author: Frank Maduri is President of LoginID

data.title: Zepic Launches Agentic Conversational Storefront for Consumer Brands
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Zepic’s Neura replaces the typical eight-step path to purchase with one conversation that starts from an ad, a search result or a message.
  • Neura runs as a single agent across recommendations, sales and support, connecting to tools like Shopify, Magento, CRM and POS systems and pointing shoppers to nearby stores when items are out of stock online.

Zepic, an AI-led context and engagement platform, is now offering Neura, an end-to-end AI agent that gives brands a conversational storefront the moment their customers show intent to explore, buy, or get help.

Shoppers show interest whenever they see an ad, open a post, or get a message. Getting from that moment to the right product takes about eight steps: visit, browse, search, compare, add to cart, add complementary products, check out, and chase order updates.

Neura collapses them into one conversation. A shopper taps the call-to-action on an ad, follows a link from a Google Business Profile listing to WhatsApp, or opens the chat on the brand’s own site, and that conversation becomes the storefront: they ask, and the brand answers, with no browsing, filtering, or chasing in between.

How Does Neura Turn a Single Conversation Into a Storefront?

By the time a shopper gets to the right product, it’s taken too long, and many have already gone,” said Naveen Venkatesan, Co-CEO of Zepic.

“So we flipped it. Wherever customers discover a brand, one tap opens a conversation that becomes the storefront, whether it starts from an ad, a search result, or a message,” said Venkatesan in a statement. “One conversation instead of eight steps. Neura acts as an extension of the brand’s store, wherever customers are, so every customer gets what they came for.”

What Makes Neura Different From Other AI Shopping Agents?

Neura replaces forms with conversations, collecting sizes, preferences, and order details inside the chat. It follows a brand’s own procedures step by step and takes actions in its tools, including Shopify, Magento, and the brand’s CRM, point-of-sale (POS) systems, and any MCP-enabled application.

For omnichannel brands, Neura brings online and offline together: when a product is sold out online, or a shopper needs it today, it checks nearby stores and points them to one that has it. When a question needs a person, it hands over to the brand’s team with the full context.

“Neura has added a new layer to how we show up for customers, almost like a frontline across our channels,” saidGokulraj G.K., Chief Marketing Officer at GoGizmo, a retail destination for smartphones and gadgets and one of Neura’s pilot customers. “Most of our customers want to know if a product is within their budget and if it’s in stock, and if it’s not in stock, Neura sends them to the nearest store that has it. It also shows us the questions it couldn’t answer from our knowledge base, so we know exactly what to add next. It’s helping us serve customers better across the business.”

Neura is available now worldwide on web chat, SMS and WhatsApp with Instagram and Voice coming soon. Learn more at neurahq.ai.

data.title: Majority of Retailers Adopting AI Faster Than They Can Govern It
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Nearly six in 10 retail leaders say their organizations are adopting AI faster than they can govern it, and only 31% have an AI kill switch.
  • Retailers trust AI outputs more than other industries do, 78% vs. 69%, but only 20% completely trust AI to operate without unacceptable risk or to comply with regulations.

Research commissioned by ABBYY shows that nearly six in ten retail leaders say their organizations are adopting AI faster than they can govern it, and just 31% have an AI kill switch to stop a malfunctioning system.

Retailers appear more confident overall in AI than their peers, with 78% saying they trust AI to produce accurate outputs, compared with 69% across other industries. However, that confidence weakens the issues that matter most for governance. Only 20% of retail leaders completely trust AI to operate without introducing unacceptable risks. Similarly, just 20% completely trust AI to comply with applicable regulations, well below the 29% cross-industry average.

The ABBYY Who Answers for AI: The Governance Gap report, conducted by Opinium Research, surveyed 1,200 senior managers in businesses of 100 or more employees located in the U.S., UK, France, Germany, Australia, and Singapore.

What Do Retailers Need to Close the AI Governance Gap?

Roman Kilun, Chief Compliance Officer at ABBYY, noted businesses are embracing AI, but many are still struggling with key questions around accountability, governance and ROI.

“Senior management need to do a better job of communicating what their responsible AI policies are companywide,” said Kilun in a statement. “In addition, AI requires organizations to know where data comes from, whether it can be trusted, how it can be used, and where it is stored and processed.”

Confidence In AI Masks Gaps In Trust, Compliance, Risk

Regulatory uncertainty ranks as the single biggest barrier to achieving greater ROI from AI in retail, cited by 16% of respondents. Integration with existing systems (15%) and the cost of implementation (15%) follow closely, while skills shortages and data quality each rank as one of the top challenges for 12% of retailers. For organizations that handle large volumes of customer, payment, and loyalty data, risks that carry direct consequences for brand trust include

  • 43% cite AI-generated cyberattacks as their top AI-related security risk
  • 38% are mindful of confidential data leakage
  • 32% cite insider misuse of AI.

Human oversight in retail falls short of cross-industry benchmarks. Just over half (51%) of retail leaders say humans review all important AI decisions before action is taken, compared with 56% globally Nearly a quarter (24%) say their AI systems operate largely autonomously, and 14% report no formal approach to human oversight at all, compared with 9% across industries.

Retailers lead on rollback capability, with 45% able to reverse AI changes compared with 35% across industries. Yet only 31% have an AI kill switch to stop a malfunctioning system, below the 35% average.

Retailers Split On Who Answers When AI Goes Wrong

The study reveals that retail leaders do not agree on who should take responsibility when AI systems produce harmful or incorrect outputs. More than a third (of retail leaders at businesses using AI believe the organization and the vendor should share responsibility; 27% think the organization using the AI should bear primary responsibility, while 19% place it with the AI vendor.

More than four in five retail leaders surveyed have an AI governance framework in place, and 39% say their framework is fully implemented and operational, ahead of 30% across industries. Among retailers with a framework, 81% say it has made their AI initiatives more successful, and 58% say it has made scaling AI past the pilot stage easier.

Still, 47% of retailers say their governance framework makes it easier to encourage widespread AI adoption among employees, compared with 59% across industries. In addition, 27% rate their processes for auditing AI systems for compliance, fairness, and transparency as inadequate.

“Organizations we work with are moving beyond pilots and proofs of concept into execution, and clear governance frameworks and a shared understanding of responsibility are critical to building confidence in AI,” stated Kilun.

Access the full 2026 ABBYY Who Answers for AI: The Governance Gap report for more information.

data.title: The Holiday Shopping Battle Is Moving to AI.  Are Retailers Ready?
data.description:
There’s no way around the unpleasant truth: Traditional e-commerce has devolved into a fragmented, broken process. Today, when a consumer wants new headphones, for instance, they start with an ad-cluttered search engine, visit a favorite retail website, or maybe get recommendations from friends. Then they open a dozen browser tabs, dive into product specs, check reviews, and hunt for discount codes before deciding what to buy. It’s an exhausting, time-wasting process that leads many consumers to just give up or pay more because they don’t want to deal with the hassles.

As the 2026 holiday season arrives, that process just won’t cut it – for merchants or consumers. Today, a growing number of shoppers are turning to AI. They’re telling shopping assistants what they’re looking for, what they’re willing to spend, and which features matter most. Then they’ll ask it to narrow choices, compare prices, and help them decide where to buy quickly. In 2026, this isn’t your father’s (or mother’s) holiday shopping season.

This is a significant change, because much of the work prior to a purchase takes place before the shopper visits the website. According to Accenture’s 2026 holiday shopping research, nearly two-thirds of U.S. shoppers expect AI to influence at least 30% of their holiday spending. Finding deals is the top use case at 40%, followed by comparing products at 31% and deciding where to shop at 30%. These aren’t casual browsers looking for gift inspiration. They’re using AI to make decisions that retailers have traditionally worked hard to influence: which products deserve consideration, which product offers represent good value, and which merchant gets the sale.

It All Starts with a Conversation

For years, the traditional online buying journey started with keywords. The consumer typed in “best women’s running shoes” or a particular brand and model and looked at pages of results. Conversational shopping rewires that process and lets the consumer get more specific: “I need running shoes for someone with wide feet who runs three times a week, mostly on pavement. My budget is $120.”

The AI shopping assistant uses those details about fit, use, and budget to quickly narrow the options to a small list of likely choices. For retailers, this changes what it means to be “discoverable.” A product page might perform well for conventional searches by matching a popular keyword.

But when an AI assistant works on a detailed request, the quality and completeness of your product information become crucial. Does the listing describe the fit? Are specifications available? Is the price current? Can the shopper confidently determine the product will arrive on time? These are practical questions, not abstract concerns. No retailer can guarantee a place in an AI-generated recommendation, but accurate, detailed product information gives shopping tools a better foundation to understand what a retailer sells.

Making the Shortlist May Matter More than Ranking First

Retailers have spent years jockeying for prominent positions on search engine results pages, shopping ads, and online marketplaces. Those positions still matter. But AI introduces another challenge: how do you make the cut and get on the small list of products a shopper will seriously consider?

For example, suppose a consumer wants a coffee maker for less than $150. Hundreds of products meet that threshold. So when an AI assistant narrows those choices to four or five, many brands and models may never get a look. Getting onto that shortlist is a must.

That’s why it’s important to think beyond product titles and promotional descriptions. A shopper may care about how easy a coffee maker is to clean, whether it fits in kitchen cabinets, or whether replacement parts are available. Those details can distinguish one product from another.

Comparison Shopping Retains its Central Role

The dominant role of pricing isn’t going away, of course. What’s going away is the hassle required to compare offers. Previously, a shopper comparing the same television on five different websites had to juggle prices, promotions, shipping charges, delivery dates, and even cash back. AI-assisted shopping quickly brings all of those factors into one clean comparison and a ranked set of recommendations.

But don’t be fooled. That doesn’t mean the buyer’s journey simply becomes a margin-destroying race to the bottom. Discerning customers value other aspects of the purchase – such as shipping speeds, return policies, warranties, and post-sales service – that can elevate the price. But even if the product comes in at a slightly higher-than-average price, it can still be a more desirable choice when the retailer supplements that price with better delivery terms, longer warranties, and easier returns.

Loyalty matters, too. For years, retailers have pursued customer relationships in a variety of ways – apps, loyalty programs, personalized offers, email marketing, and more. Those investments aren’t irrelevant, of course, but conversational shopping introduces a different starting point. Instead of opening the retailer’s familiar app, a consumer starts with a need and asks AI to find suitable options. The retailer becomes one of several possible answers, not the default destination.

Consumers remember when a retailer delivers on time, handles a return fairly, or simplifies the checkout process. These thoughtful enhancements to the buying journey create exceptional loyalty and higher levels of trust that AI can’t replicate.

What Retailers Should Do Now

There’s no need to reinvent your entire digital strategy, but there are important steps to take when thinking about how your products appear as consumers use AI to research purchases. Use authentic shopping pathways to test several different AI assistants. What products appear? What information do those assistants use? Are the descriptions, prices, and availability accurate? Note the questions your product pages don’t answer. Keep pricing, promotions, and shipping information current. Determine how to measure visibility when discovery happens outside your channels.

Without question, AI-assisted shopping is still evolving, and even the best assistants can miss relevant products, misunderstand preferences, or present outdated information. But don’t confuse those limitations with any lack of consumer interest. The significant change is that shoppers increasingly begin with a question instead of a destination. The purchase may still happen on a retailer’s website or in its store. The decision about where to spend, however, is increasingly happening elsewhere.

Nicolas Salat-Baroux is one of the 3 co-founders of Joko, alongside Xavier and Alexandre. He currently serves as Chief Revenue Officer (CRO), where he leads the Online, Gift Cards, and Card-Linked business lines, as well as Joko’s partnerships in the U.S. Based in New York, Nicolas brings a business perspective shaped by his previous experience in M&A at Goldman Sachs, and in business development at Jumia across Africa. He is a graduate of ESSEC Business School. Passionate about retail innovation, Nicolas is on a mission to build the ultimate AI shopping app, that helps consumers find the right product for them and buy it at the best price.

data.title: AI Agents Are Browsing. Ahead of Black Friday, Retailers Need Them to Buy
data.description:
Retailers are racing to win agentic attention ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday. The question they should be asking is whether they can convert that attention into actual sales.

Every retail conversation seems to have a new audience: agents. The advice is familiar by now. Structure your product data so large language models can find it, understand it and recommend it. Let’s imagine the strategy works. Your product appears in an AI-generated answer. A shopping assistant visits your site, compares products, creates an account, or moves toward a transaction. You’ve captured a new kind of attention.

Then what? Are you ready to receive the traffic you’ve worked so hard to attract?

Attention Is Not the Same as Readiness

The first mistake is to assume agentic attention behaves like human attention.

A human visitor arrives with a browser, a device, a set of intentions and a degree of context that retailers have spent decades learning to interpret. An agent may arrive on behalf of a person, another system or no legitimate customer at all. It may be gathering information, comparing options, executing a task, testing a credential or probing for a weakness.

From the outside, those interactions can look remarkably similar. That is the central tension in the agentic internet: the traffic that looks like a promising new customer may also be automated abuse wearing the shape of a promising new customer.

The question is not simply whether an interaction claims to be ChatGPT, Claude or another recognized agent. Names and user-agent strings are not identity. They can be copied, manipulated or used as camouflage. A request presenting itself as a familiar AI assistant may be a legitimate agent acting for a real buyer. It may also be a spoofed system, a scraper or a fraud operation using AI because it knows businesses are eager to welcome machine-driven demand.

And the landscape is already more varied than the phrase “AI agent” suggests. Cloud agents, agentic browsers and browser extensions can all reach the same digital property, sometimes through nearly indistinguishable paths.90% of agentic traffic observed by HUMAN is stealth by default. The traffic does not arrive carrying a reliable badge that tells a retailer what it is, who authorized it or what it intends to do.

Influencing an Order Is Not the Same as Completing One

Salesforce reported that AI and agents influenced 20% of all global orders during Cyber Week 2025. That number has shaped a lot of planning for this season, and the verb matters: influencing an order and completing one are not the same thing.

DoorDash offered the clearest illustration. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call, CEO Tony Xu was asked about agent-based ordering. His answer: “we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents.” Several hundred, at a company that completes roughly three million deliveries a day.

That tracks with what latest trends in agentic traffic: across September, 60.4% of agentic activity went to ecommerce sites, 81% of it landed on search and product pages, and 2.4% reached checkout. Meta’s Muse, which arrived at number one in its first month, sent 76.5% of its traffic to ecommerce and converted 2.6% of it.

So agents are arriving in volume and browsing intensively, but they are very rarely buying. For retailers heading into Black Friday and Cyber Monday, that gap is the whole story, because agentic traffic is already shaping the numbers you use to judge performance without showing up in the revenue those numbers are meant to explain. Page views inflate. Measured conversion falls. Neither movement tells you anything about demand.

Routing Matters More Than Welcoming

The next phase of agentic commerce will not be defined by whether retailers let automated traffic in. It will be defined by whether they can route different kinds of traffic intelligently.

Different participants need different experiences:

  • A human buyer may need a rich, persuasive journey
  • A legitimate agent may need clear product data, structured policies, inventory information and a reliable path to act on its user’s behalf
  • A training crawler may be governed by a content-access policy
  • A suspicious interaction may deserve additional verification
  • A malicious operation should be stopped

This is why “block or allow” is becoming an inadequate operating model. It treats every automated interaction as interchangeable at exactly the moment automation is becoming more diverse, more commercially important and harder to distinguish by appearance alone.

It also requires marketing, security and fraud teams to share more than a meeting. Without shared definitions and shared accountability, marketing celebrates a surge in agentic traffic that security experiences as an attack wave.

Four Actions for Retailers Before Black Friday

None of this has to wait for a new platform or budget cycle.

  1. Establish a baseline now, while the week is still ordinary. If you don’t know what share of your traffic is agentic today, you will have nothing to read your Cyber Week numbers against.
  2. Separate agentic activity in your reporting rather than letting it blend into the totals, so conversion and engagement stay interpretable when volume spikes.
  3. Decide in advance which agents get which access, and be specific: browsing, account creation, authentication, checkout. Those are different permissions, and peak week is a poor time to be making the call live.
  4. Agree who owns the decision when marketing and security disagree. That conversation is uncomfortable in November and nearly impossible in December.

The Takeaway

Traditional retail metrics were built around human visibility. Sessions, add-to-carts and conversion rates remain useful, but become harder to read when a growing share of activity is mediated by an agent. A page view may be a crawler collecting competitive pricing. A completed transaction may be legitimate commerce, an unauthorized purchase, or a test of stolen payment credentials.

Being mentioned by an AI system isn’t the same as being chosen by a customer, and being chosen by an agent isn’t the same as being ready to serve, verify and retain the customer behind it.

In the agentic internet, attention is only the beginning. The advantage will belong to the retailers who can recognize what arrives, route it responsibly, convert it safely and tell the difference between activity and growth.

Sarah Acker is SVP and Global Head of Marketing at HUMAN Security, where she leads worldwide marketing strategy spanning brand, creative, communications and product marketing. She writes regularly on agentic traffic, measurement and digital trust.
data.author: Sarah Acker, SVP and Global Head of Marketing, HUMAN Security

data.title: Ahold Delhaize USA Advances Next-Generation In-Store Experience
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Ahold Delhaize USA is using NCR Voyix’s Voyix Commerce Platform to modernize point-of-sale, self-checkout, pharmacy and fuel operations across its grocery brands, with new POS technology already live in 100 stores.
  • The multi-year rollout aims to create a more consistent technology foundation for customers and associates while keeping the flexibility each local brand needs to serve its shoppers.

Ahold Delhaize USA announced a next step in modernizing the technology that supports its grocery brands, helping create a more connected, efficient and customer-focused shopping experience.

The grocer will leverage technology from NCR Voyix to deliver faster, more seamless experiences for customers and associates.

The modernization effort spans key store capabilities including point-of-sale, self-checkout, pharmacy and fuel operations. It builds on years of work to streamline platforms and create greater consistency, while supporting local brand differentiation.

What Is Ahold Delhaize USA’s In-Store Technology Strategy?

Ann Dozier, Chief Information Officer for Ahold Delhaize USA, stated their technology strategy is focused on making it easier for customers to shop and and easier for associates to serve their customers.

“Our goal is to create a more consistent technology foundation and a more connected experience, while maintaining the flexibility that allows each of our local brands to meet its customers’ needs in the short term and positions us for the future,” said Dozier. “The rollout is underway with new point-of-sale technology now available in 100 stores, with the rollout continuing over the next several years.”

Why Did Ahold Delhaize USA Choose the Voyix Commerce Platform?

The selection of the Voyix Commerce Platform builds on Ahold Delhaize USA’s long-standing relationship with NCR Voyix, whose technology has supported the company’s operations for many years.

NCR Voyix is a global platform-powered leader in unified commerce for shopping and dining. Combining a flexible, intelligent platform with end-to-end payments capabilities and services developed through its deep industry experience, Voyix empowers retailers and restaurants to accelerate new possibilities for their operations, experiences and business outcomes.

“We’re proud to continue supporting Ahold Delhaize USA and its brands as they advance their technology modernization strategies,” said James G. Kelly, President and Chief Executive Officer of NCR Voyix. “Modern retailers need a technology foundation that can simplify store operations while giving them the flexibility to innovate as customer expectations evolve. This multi-year modernization demonstrates the role our next-generation platform can play in enabling transformation at enterprise scale.”

How Does This Rollout Fit Into Ahold Delhaize USA’s Broader Technology Plans?

The advancement builds on previous technology improvements at Ahold Delhaize USA, including the launch of the company’s proprietary e-commerce platform, the deployment of a proprietary retail media advertising platform and the integration of the digital, data and technology teams at Ahold Delhaize USA into a unified technology organization for the future.

The rollout is part of Ahold Delhaize USA’s broader strategy to simplify its technology landscape, strengthen shared capabilities and support the distinct strategies of its local brands.

“At the end of the day, technology is only as good as the value it provides to the business and to customers. Working with our brands and technology partners, we look forward to continuing to deliver more value for our businesses and support their growth in an increasingly competitive marketplace,” added Dozier.
data.author: james.hickey

data.title: Peak Season Now Has Two Kinds of Traffic
data.description:
Every retailer plans for the holiday spike. This year, the spike has a second layer that retail and ecommerce website leads should understand.

Adobe expects U.S. online holiday sales to reach $275.1 billion, and it expects AI-referred traffic to retail sites to grow 130% year over year, with the biggest jumps on Thanksgiving and Black Friday. The RealReal has just rolled out its AI shopping agent to all 45 million members. And retailers still don’t agree on whether these agents are welcome at all. Amazon sued Perplexity last year to stop its browser agent from making purchases on shoppers’ behalf.

Whatever side a retailer lands on, the infrastructure question is pretty much the same. Peak season now brings two kinds of visitors, people and the software shopping for them, and the two don’t behave the same way.

AI Agents Don’t Browse Like People

When a living, breathing human lands on a product page, they scroll, and maybe open two more tabs. An AI agent comparing options for a shopper can request dozens of product and category pages in seconds, across several stores at once. That agent doesn’t wait patiently either. Agents that fetch pages on demand work with short timeouts, and a page that loads slowly or not at all is simply skipped.

That traffic gets piled on top of the human peak, not instead of it. A site that’s been scaled for last year’s busiest day may not have the headroom it needs the next time around.

Decide Your Bot Policy Before The Spike

Not all automated traffic is the same. Search and citation crawlers help shoppers find you. An agent fetching a page because a shopper asked it a question is, in effect, the shopper. Other bots collect website content to train AI models without directing customers back to the site. Treating all automated traffic the same can mean blocking potential shoppers while allowing bots that offer little value to consume website resources.

Make the decision deliberately, write it into your rules, and remember that a robots.txt file is a request, not a lock. Bots that ignore it need to be handled at the firewall or CDN. We’ve written up how to block or welcome bots and AI crawlers, and most of it applies on any host.

Check That Your Firewall Isn’t Turning Away Buyers

Bot protection is tuned to stop scrapers and credential stuffing, which is the right priority most of the year. But the same rules can challenge or block an agent that is trying to load a product page for a real shopper. Rate limits written for scrapers can cut off legitimate comparison traffic at exactly the moment it matters.

Before your next peak, review firewall and bot-management logs for blocked requests on product, search and checkout pages. If legitimate agents are being challenged, adjust the rules now, while there’s time to test the change.

Speed For Machines, Freshness For Prices

For agents, server response time matters more than how fast a page looks finished in a browser. Caching product and category pages at the edge is the most effective way to keep response times low under load.

The catch is that agents will also quote prices and stock to shoppers. A cached page with yesterday’s price can turn a sale into a complaint. Short cache lifetimes for price and stock data, and purging the cache automatically when they change, let you keep both speed and accuracy.

Load-test the real peak. Most load tests hit the homepage. Real holiday traffic hits search, category filters, inventory lookups and checkout, which are the parts that can’t be served from cache. Test those, at a volume that includes automated traffic, and include the third-party scripts and payment services your checkout depends on. One slow external script can hold up an otherwise healthy page.

Watch the right signals during the rush. During peak days, separate automated and human traffic in your analytics and logs so one doesn’t hide problems in the other. Set alerts for checkout errors, sudden spikes in blocked requests and server response time, not only on whether the site is up. And make sure someone who can change a firewall rule or purge a cache is on call through the busiest days.

No need to pick a side yet. The debate over whether AI agents should be allowed to shop on people’s behalf won’t be settled this season. Retailers don’t need to settle it either. What they need is a deliberate decision about which traffic they want, infrastructure that reflects that decision, and enough headroom to handle both kinds of visitors at once.

The retailers who struggle this year won’t be the ones who chose the wrong side. They’ll be the ones who never noticed the second wave of traffic until it arrived.

Nickola Naous is co-founder and CTO of Flashcloud, a web hosting company. He has nearly two decades of experience building and running hosting infrastructure, and writes about performance, security and how websites handle AI-driven traffic.
data.author: Nickola Naous, Co-founder and CTO, Flashcloud

data.title: Americans Turning to AI for Holiday Shopping Help: Visa
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • Visa’s 2026 Holiday Spending Shift Survey finds that 54% of U.S. adults have used AI for at least one shopping task, up from 47% last year, and 41% wouldn’t tell someone that AI helped choose their gift.
  • Shoppers readily use AI to compare prices and find deals, but only 23% trust GenAI to handle payments, while 61% trust Visa to secure an AI-powered payment.

Secret Sant-AI?

Research recently release from Visa finds 41% of Americans wouldn’t tell someone that AI helped choose their gift, as more shoppers quietly hand AI the job of finding gifts and tracking down deals.

The findings come from Visa’s 2026 Holiday Spending Shift Survey paints a picture of consumers juggling persistent cost pressures, evolving technology and heightened fraud concerns, while still finding ways to check every box on their gift lists. More than half of U.S. adults (54%) have already used AI for at least one shopping task, up from 47% last year.

How Are Consumers Approaching Holiday Shopping This Year?

“Consumers are approaching the holidays with both value and security in mind,” said Michael Brown, principal U.S. economist at Visa.

“They’re looking for deals, experimenting with tools like AI and changing how they shop in response to fraud concern,” said Brown in a statement. “It’s a consumer who is adapting as the shopping experience itself continues to change.”

How Are Shoppers Using AI While Guarding Against Fraud?

The convenience of digital shopping comes with growing unease about scams. Nearly three in 10 shoppers say they were targeted by fraud during last year’s holiday season, a figure that rises to 39% among Gen Z. In response, three-quarters of Americans have changed how they shop: enabling two-factor authentication (34%), changing passwords more often (34%), declining to save payment details (25%), switching from debit to credit cards (24%) and using digital wallets (21%).

The report found that shoppers are most comfortable handing AI the practical tasks: comparing prices (61%), checking availability (59%), finding discounts (57%) and suggesting gift ideas (54%). Nearly a quarter say they’re more comfortable using AI for shopping than they were last year. Gen Z is leading the shift. More than eight in 10 young consumers are open to AI assistance, and 73% would let it suggest gift ideas — 19 points higher than adults overall.

Cost-conscious shopping isn’t going anywhere as 84% of respondents stated they’ve taken at least one action to manage higher everyday costs in the past year — most commonly hunting for discounts (47%), cutting discretionary spending (35%) and trading down to lower-cost brands (33%).

Will Consumers Trust AI to Make Purchases for Them?

But there’s a gap between browsing and buying. While consumers are increasingly comfortable using AI assistants for discovery, research and decision-making, trusting one to make a purchase is a bigger leap — only 23% of U.S. consumers trust GenAI to handle payment transactions on their behalf, according to Visa’s Trust Index. It’s a familiar pattern: the technology often arrives before consumers fully trust the experience, similar to when payments moved online and again when commerce went mobile.

What shifts the equation? Familiar brands. The Trust Index found that 61% of consumers trust Visa to secure an AI-powered payment — rising to 68% among 18–34-year-olds and 71% among weekly AI users. As agentic commerce grows, that confidence may be what bridges the gap between AI as a shopping assistant and AI as a shopping agent.

Besides cash, when it comes to gifts, Americans are dreaming of experiences. Travel (60%) and live-event tickets (55%) top the list of what people are most excited to give or receive. But actually buying gifts tells a different story. Only 15% of respondents are prioritizing experiences, while 27% are focused on physical items. Gen Z comes closest to aligning their wallets with their wishes– 39% are splitting spending evenly between the two, compared to 26% of all adults.

Are Consumers Ready to Pay With Stablecoins, Crypto?

Stablecoins are still new to many Americans, but more than half (56%) see a benefit, rising to 77% of Gen Z. Among Americans who send money abroad, 51% say that after seeing the benefits, they are likely to use stablecoins in the next year.

Crypto resonates with the same groups. Half of those who send money abroad (51%) call it a useful way to do so, against 26% of adults. Gen Z is more comfortable shopping with a retailer that accepts crypto (34% vs. 25%).

“Consumers are navigating a lot this season, from higher costs, new technology and real concerns about fraud,” said Brown. “But they’re adapting. They’re hunting for deals, shopping smarter and staying alert. That resilience is the real story.”
data.author: james.hickey

data.title: Retail Media’s NASCAR Problem Is Costing Retailers Holiday Revenue
data.description:
Every holiday season, retailers face enormous pressure to squeeze more revenue out of the gifting-driven surge in their web traffic.

This creates an obvious temptation: Advertisers want more exposure, shoppers are spending more time on the site, why not create more places to advertise? The problem is that eventually the store starts to look like a NASCAR stock car, with logos covering every available inch until you can barely see what is underneath.

A lot of retail sites are starting to approach advertising in much the same way.

Why More Ad Placements Can Hurt the Shopping Experience

Incremental sponsored placements can make money for the retailer without actually providing value to the shopper. If someone repeatedly sees sponsored products that have little to do with what they are actually looking for, they grow suspicious of anything labeled “Sponsored,” and eventually learn to ignore them.

This becomes especially important during the holidays because discovery is such a big part of how people shop. Someone might arrive knowing they need a gift for a teenager, a new television for the family or a toy for a niece or nephew without knowing the exact product they want.

Holiday Discovery Depends on Relevance, Not Volume

A sponsored product that introduces someone to an item they want to buy is doing its job: the shopper finds something useful, the advertiser gets a sale and the retailer makes advertising revenue.

Amazon is an example of this cycle at work. The retail giant has built advertising deeply into the shopping experience, with sponsored products appearing across search, browse and product pages, all designed around what someone is searching for or likely to buy. This relevance is what lets advertising natively become part of discovery.

The mistake other retailers make is copying the number of ads Amazon shows without first getting the relevance right.

Part of the reason for this imbalance is that most retail media systems make ad density easy and relevance hard. Many historically ranked ads primarily by keyword match and bid, so the slot went to the highest bidder whether or not that shopper was likely to buy. But relevance at scale is a prediction problem, and machine learning — trained on signals from real purchase behavior — is well-suited to address it. Retailers can now access this capability through partners rather than building it in-house.

Why Retail Media Revenue Grows When Ads Match Shopper Intent

After their first four weeks with Moloco, the majority of our retailers have at least doubled the ad revenue they earn on each dollar of merchandise sales. When ads are relevant and match what shoppers want, shoppers keep clicking and advertisers keep spending.

That is why relevance is going to matter more than ad density as retail media grows. Density executed effectively is an output of relevance. If retailers get better at predicting what someone actually wants to buy, they can show more advertising without making the experience worse.

And there is a lot of room for retailers to grow here: search results, product pages and other parts of the store serve different purposes, so the advertising should behave differently in each.

The pressure to get this right will be even higher during the holidays, when retailers are trying to capture as much revenue as possible while demand is high. There will always be another advertiser willing to pay for another placement, but retailers should be careful about taking that money if the ad makes the store worse for the person trying to shop there. Otherwise, they risk ending up with a lot of logos on the car and a shopper who has learned to tune all of them out.

Pat Copeland is General Manager of Moloco Commerce Media, where he leads strategy, product innovation and growth for the company’s AI-powered commerce advertising business. He brings more than 30 years of experience in machine learning, advertising and enterprise software, having held leadership roles at Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Zendesk, including helping launch and scale Amazon’s Sponsored Brands into a multibillion-dollar advertising platform.
data.author: Pat Copeland, General Manager of Moloco Commerce Media
